lessons.title: Market Cap & Circulating Supply
lessons.description: Understand how crypto market size is measured and why supply matters.

content.text: How Big Is a Cryptocurrency?

**Market capitalization (market cap)** is the most common way to measure a cryptocurrency's size. It's calculated simply:

**Market Cap = Price × Circulating Supply**

For example: if Bitcoin trades at $60,000 and there are 19.5 million BTC in circulation, Bitcoin's market cap is $1.17 trillion.
📊 Supply Types

**Circulating supply** — Coins currently available and tradeable in the market.

**Total supply** — All coins that exist, including locked or unreleased ones.

**Max supply** — The maximum coins that will ever exist (e.g. Bitcoin's hard cap is 21 million).

**Fully Diluted Valuation (FDV)** — Market cap calculated using the maximum possible supply. FDV shows the theoretical future size of a project.
👑 Bitcoin Dominance

**Bitcoin dominance** is Bitcoin's market cap as a percentage of the entire crypto market. When dominance is high, Bitcoin is leading. When it falls, altcoins are often outperforming — this is called **altcoin season**.

**Market cap tiers:**
- Large cap (>$10B): Bitcoin, Ethereum — more stable
- Mid cap ($1B–$10B): established altcoins
- Small cap (<$1B): higher risk, higher potential reward

lessons.title: Order Books & Liquidity
lessons.description: Learn how trades happen on exchanges — bids, asks, spreads, and why liquidity matters.

content.text: The Engine Behind Every Trade
Every trade on a traditional exchange goes through an **order book** — a real-time list of all pending buy and sell orders. Understanding order books helps you buy and sell at better prices.
📖 Bids, Asks & the Spread

**Bid** — the highest price a buyer is willing to pay right now.
**Ask** — the lowest price a seller will accept right now.
**Spread** — the gap between bid and ask. A tight spread means high liquidity; a wide spread means low liquidity.

**Order types:**
- **Market order** — buy/sell immediately at the current best price
- **Limit order** — set a specific price; the order only fills if the market reaches it
💧 Liquidity & Slippage

**Liquidity** is how easily you can buy or sell an asset without moving its price. High liquidity = easy to trade, tight spreads. Low liquidity = large orders can move the price significantly.

**Slippage** happens when your large order moves through multiple price levels, so you end up paying more (or selling for less) than expected. This is especially common in low-liquidity markets.

lessons.title: CEX vs DEX
lessons.description: Compare centralized and decentralized exchanges — and understand the tradeoffs.

content.text: Where Do People Actually Buy Crypto?

Most people buy crypto on exchanges. There are two fundamentally different types: **Centralized Exchanges (CEX)** run by companies, and **Decentralized Exchanges (DEX)** run by smart contracts. Each has real advantages and real risks.
🏢 Centralized Exchanges (CEX)

CEXes like Coinbase, Binance, and Kraken are run by companies. They:
- Require KYC (government ID verification)
- Hold your private keys (custodial)
- Are user-friendly with fiat on-ramps
- Are regulated and insured to varying degrees

**Risk:** If the exchange is hacked, goes bankrupt, or freezes withdrawals, you could lose your funds. FTX's 2022 collapse lost users billions.
🔄 Decentralized Exchanges (DEX)

DEXes like Uniswap and PancakeSwap use smart contracts and **Automated Market Makers (AMMs)** instead of order books. Trades happen directly between users' wallets — the exchange never holds your funds.

- No KYC required
- Non-custodial (you keep your keys)
- Access to any token, including new/obscure ones
- Slightly more complex for beginners

lessons.title: Bull & Bear Markets
lessons.description: Understand market cycles, sentiment terms, and how to recognize market phases.

content.text: Markets Move in Cycles

Crypto markets don't move in a straight line. They cycle between periods of rising prices (**bull markets**) and falling prices (**bear markets**). Understanding which phase you're in helps you make better decisions — and avoid costly emotional mistakes.
🐂 Bull Markets

A **bull market** is a sustained period of rising prices, optimism, and strong investor confidence. In crypto, bull markets have seen coins rise 1,000%+. Key emotions: **FOMO** (Fear Of Missing Out) drives people to buy at the top.

**Crypto-specific signals:**
- Bitcoin makes new all-time highs
- Mainstream media covers crypto positively
- New user signups on exchanges spike
🐻 Bear Markets & Crypto Winter

A **bear market** is a sustained decline of 20%+ from recent highs. **Crypto winter** refers to an extended bear market lasting many months. Key emotions: **FUD** (Fear, Uncertainty, Doubt) drives panic selling.

**Capitulation** — the moment when remaining investors give up and sell at a loss — often marks the market bottom. Experienced investors use this as a buying signal.

**Altcoin season** — a period in bull markets when altcoins outperform Bitcoin significantly.

lessons.title: Reading Price Charts
lessons.description: Learn to read candlestick charts, identify trends, and understand key indicators.

content.text: Charts Are the Language of Markets

Price charts are the primary tool traders use to understand market behavior. The most common chart type is the **candlestick chart**, where each candle shows the price action for a specific time period — from 1 minute to 1 week.
🕯️ Reading a Candlestick

Each candle shows four prices:
- **Open** — price at the start of the period
- **Close** — price at the end of the period
- **High** — the highest price reached
- **Low** — the lowest price reached

**Green candle** = close > open (price went up)
**Red candle** = close < open (price went down)
**Wick** (shadow) = the thin line showing the high/low range beyond the body
📊 Key Chart Concepts

**Support** — A price level where buying has historically stopped a decline. Think of it as a floor.
**Resistance** — A price level where selling has historically stopped a rise. Think of it as a ceiling.
**Volume** — How much of an asset was traded. High volume confirms moves; low volume signals weak conviction.
**Moving average** — Smooths price data over a period (e.g. 50-day MA) to show the trend direction.
**RSI** — Relative Strength Index (0–100). Above 70 = overbought, below 30 = oversold.
